title: In the Weeds: Standards-Based Instruction
author: Ben Zulauf
summary: Zulauf argues that standards-based instruction — in which lesson objectives are stated as discrete reading skills ('identify central idea,' 'determine point of view') — is structurally ineffective because it asks students to practice decontextualized moves without the domain knowledge those moves require. Using a worked example from a Core Knowledge Language Arts lesson on the Catholic Reformation, he shows how knowledge-centered lesson planning differs: objectives specify what students will know about the content, not what skill they will practice; questions are sorted into 'must ask' (tightly aligned to content objectives) and 'may ask' (generative but peripheral); and teachers pre-analyze the text for features that might interrupt comprehension — complex pronouns, long sentences, ellipses requiring inference. Zulauf draws on Willingham's insight that starting with a question rather than a statement of content piques curiosity and drives deeper encoding. He closes by arguing that when teachers internalize the text this thoroughly, their working memory during instruction is freed to attend fully to what students are actually saying rather than managing what comes next — producing markedly smoother and more responsive teaching.
points: Standards-based objectives ('identify central idea', 'determine point of view') are structurally deficient because they treat skills as the learning goal rather than the content knowledge from which skilled reading actually emerges; knowledge-centered objectives specify what students will understand about the domain, not what reading move they will practice.

Sorting lesson questions into 'must ask' (tightest alignment to content objectives) and 'may ask' (educationally valid but peripheral) allows teachers to allocate response-demand strategies — mini whiteboards, think-ink-pair-share — precisely where collective cognitive effort matters most, rather than spreading it across every question equally.

Text pre-analysis — identifying every sentence feature likely to interrupt comprehension (pronoun referents, complex conjunctions, multi-clause sentences) — is the preparation step that separates teachers who can respond fluently to errors from those who are caught off guard and lose instructional momentum.

Starting with a question rather than a content objective ('Why did some people believe the Church needed to be reformed?') is more than pedagogical style: citing Willingham, Zulauf argues that a question piques curiosity in ways that a stated answer cannot, shaping both motivation and the quality of initial encoding.

When a teacher has internalized the text so thoroughly — knowing the key content, where it appears, what makes it hard, and what response they need before moving on — working memory during instruction is freed to attend fully to what students are saying, producing the kind of smooth, responsive teaching that looks effortless from the outside.
quotes: Standards-based grading leads to standards-based instruction, which leads to teachers trying to teach standards in isolation. 'This week, we're focusing on central idea. Next week, it's point of view. In two weeks, we'll discuss cause and effect.' This type of instruction simply isn't effective.

In this reading lesson, we know before getting to the text what knowledge we want students to walk away having. If you use a curriculum that does not provide this knowledge and instead provides generic skills as the goal for the lesson, students miss the content that would have made the skill meaningful.

Sometimes I think that we, as teachers, are so eager to get to the answers that we do not devote sufficient time to developing the question. But it's the question that piques people's interest. Being told an answer doesn't do anything for you. When you plan a lesson, you start with the information you want students to know by its end.

Learning happens when people have to think hard. Therefore, I will need to use strategies that require everyone to do the work such as responding on mini whiteboards or think, ink, pair, share when I pose these.

In just this one section, we have around 10 things that might interrupt comprehension. We certainly don't have time to ask questions or provide instruction about each, but we can pull out some of the more important ones.
The first step in preparing for a lesson is to internalize the text that you're teaching. You can't help students internalize information if you don't even understand the enduring understandings.

If a teacher's working memory is the real bottleneck in instruction, consider how much better your instruction could be when you've planned this much in advance. And if I feel better about my instruction and the kids are learning more, then this is the path I'll continue to take.” Archived from Challenge Accepted!
